TurboQuant by Google Made it Possible to Run HUGE Models Locally

Shreyansh Jain

It unveils a 5x KV cache compression breakthrough, enabling efficient local AI while sending memory market stocks into a tailspin.

Before starting going deep into the paper lets first understand why the timing of this paper is so perfect.

The Memory Crisis Nobody Saw Coming

The three companies that make virtually all the world’s DRAM , Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have quietly abandoned the consumer market. The reason is simple: AI data centers are far more profitable customers, and manufacturers are dedicating production lines entirely to High Bandwidth Memory for AI accelerators. The result? DRAM prices are up 171% year-over-year, with DDR5 spot prices having quadrupled since September 2025. Micron has formally exited the consumer RAM market, leaving effectively two global suppliers. Intel’s CEO has stated there will be no relief until 2028.

For anyone wanting to run LLMs locally, this isn’t a temporary inconvenience it’s a structural wall. And that’s exactly the problem TurboQuant was built to solve.

Google’s DeepSeek Moment

On March 24, 2026, Google Research dropped TurboQuant a compression algorithm that reduces KV cache memory overhead with absolute quality neutrality at 3.5 bits per channel, achieving this with no retraining required on any transformer architecture. The internet immediately called it Google’s Pied Piper. But Cloudflare’s CEO called it something more precise.

Some industry leaders are calling this Google’s DeepSeek moment a reference to how DeepSeek shocked the AI world by achieving competitive results at a fraction of the compute cost. The parallel is apt: just as DeepSeek proved that intelligence doesn’t require brute-force spending, TurboQuant proves that what the industry was struggling to achieve through physical scaling, Google achieved through mathematics. Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron stocks fell sharply on the news because when a memory reduction exceeding 4x or 5x ships as pure software, the entire “buy more RAM” thesis starts to crack.

The Problem With Running LLMs Locally

Most people’s laptops ship with 8GB or 16GB of RAM. That’s not a complaint that’s the market reality for students, developers in emerging economies, and anyone who hasn’t spent north of $1,500 on a machine. And it creates a hard ceiling the moment you want to run anything meaningful locally.

Here’s what the numbers actually look like. A 7B model at 4-bit quantization needs roughly 3.5-4GB of VRAM , manageable. But the same model at full 16-bit precision demands 14GB impractical for most consumer GPUs. Step up to a 13B model and you’re at 7GB at 4-bit, jumping to 26GB at full precision. These aren’t edge cases , these are the models people actually want to run for coding, reasoning, and summarization.

The capability gap is real too. A 4B model handles simple Q&A and basic chat it will not write production code or reason through a complex problem. A 7B model can write clean Python with basic error handling. A 13B model does the same but with optimized logic and better context awareness. The jump in output quality between 7B and 13B is meaningful. But that jump costs you double the memory and in a RAM crisis, double the memory means double the price.

Then there’s the KV cache problem, which sits on top of all of this. A 4B model needs roughly 3GB of KV cache at a 32K context window. An 8B model climbs to ~5GB at the same context. A 70B model exceeds 42GB at 128K context the KV cache alone. That’s before you’ve even loaded the model weights. On an 8GB machine, you’re not hitting memory limits you’re running into a wall from the very first long conversation.

The Memory Tax of Remembering

At the heart of every modern LLM is the attention mechanism the idea that when a model processes a word, it doesn’t read it in isolation. It weighs that word against every other word it has seen, asking: what context matters here? This is what makes transformers powerful. It is also what makes them expensive.

To avoid recomputing these relationships on every single new token which would be catastrophically slow models cache the intermediate results. Specifically, they store two matrices at every layer: the Keys and the Values. This is the KV cache. Think of it as the model’s working scratchpad every token it reads gets written into this scratchpad so future tokens can reference it without redoing the math.

The problem is the bill. The KV cache grows linearly with every token in the context. Longer conversation, bigger document, more context more memory consumed, continuously. At 32K context on an 8B model, the KV cache alone eats roughly 5GB. At 128K context, over 20GB before the model weights have even loaded.

Why Every Compression Algorithm Before This Was Broken

Vectors are fundamental to the operation of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Transformers, as their core attention mechanisms rely heavily on high-dimensional vector operations. However, during text generation, storing the Key and Value (KV) embeddings for every past token creates a massive memory bottleneck, which severely increases inference latency and slows down compute times. Vector Quantization (VQ) addresses this by compressing these vectors within the Euclidean space. It reduces the memory footprint of each vector by shrinking the bit-precision of its individual coordinates (e.g., from floating-point numbers to low-bit integers), all while keeping the total number of dimensions exactly the same. This preserves the geometric structure needed for attention operations while vastly improving computational efficiency.

But the question which arises is ‘What is the minimum number of bits needed to represent data without losing information?’

The solution to this question was given long back in 1948 by Claude Shannon and his Source Coding Theory in the field of Information Theory. Shannon mathematically proved that the absolute limit for lossless compression is defined by the data’s entropy a measure of the inherent unpredictability or true information content of the source. You cannot compress data using fewer bits than its entropy without permanently losing information.

However, Vector Quantization (VQ) for LLMs is inherently lossy; we intentionally trade perfect floating-point precision for smaller integer sizes to save memory. To address this, Shannon’s work established the distortion-rate function. This provides a mathematical floor for lossy compression: it calculates the absolute minimum amount of geometric error (like Mean Squared Error) that you must accept for any given bit-width budget.

The brilliance of modern methods like TurboQuant is that they don’t just compress well practically but also mathematically prove that their compression error sits just a tiny fraction above this absolute theoretical floor defined by Shannon.

As LLM capabilities depend heavily on their model size and context length serving them requires substantial memory demands and increased inference latency. This latency is primarily attributed to communication bottlenecks between HBM and SRAM on accelerators, or across distributed clusters. By compressing or quantizing model weights and activations, we can effectively mitigate these bottlenecks, resulting in significant reductions in inference costs

TurboQuant Core

Every vector quantization method before TurboQuant faced the same fundamental tradeoff: compress aggressively and lose accuracy, or preserve accuracy and carry expensive memory overhead. Existing approaches either lacked accelerator compatibility making them too slow for real-time KV cache quantization or stayed frustratingly far from the theoretical compression limit Shannon defined. TurboQuant was built to break both constraints simultaneously.

It is a lightweight, online-capable compression algorithm meaning it compresses vectors as they arrive, with no pre-training, no calibration dataset, and no model-specific tuning and is highly accelerator-friendly, a critical requirement for production AI workloads. Google Research

The architecture is a deliberate two-stage pipeline.

Stage 1 PolarQuant handles the bulk of compression with near-zero overhead.

Stage 2 QJL acts as a 1-bit mathematical error corrector on whatever PolarQuant leaves behind. Together, they push compression to within a fraction of what Shannon’s information theory says is even theoretically possible.

PolarQuant Compressing Direction, Not Magnitude

Imagine we have a tiny 5-dimensional Key vector sitting in our KV cache. In LLMs, it is very common for vectors to have “outliers” one or two coordinates that are massive, while the rest are tiny.

Let’s say our input vector (x) looks like this: x = [10.0,0.1,−0.2,0.0,0.1]

If you want to compress this vector, you have a massive headache:

TurboQuant multiplies the input vector by a random rotation matrix mathematically smearing the energy spike evenly across all dimensions without changing the vector’s total magnitude.

When you spin this vector in space, that massive 10.0 spike doesn't just disappear; its energy gets mathematically smeared across all the other coordinates. The new rotated vector (y = ∏• x) might look like this: y = [4.5, -4.2, 3.8, 5.1, -4.6]

The MSE-optimal quantizer starts by randomly rotating d-dimensional input vectors (Keys and Values). Observing the key fact that each coordinate in the rotated vectors follows a Beta distribution, a optimal Lloyd-Max quantizer was designed for each coordinate by solving a continuous k-means problem. This method gives optimal MSE distortion bound and minimizes the L2 norm of the residual.

Lloyd-Max quantizer basically talks about Finding the best set of quantization levels that minimize error (MSE).

Beta distribution is a highly flexible probability distribution that models outcomes confined within a strict, finite range most commonly between 0 and 1 (or shifted to -1 and 1). Often called as “probability distribution of probabilities”

QJL-Killing the Bias With One Bit

To obtain an unbiased and low-distortion quantizer for inner products, they compose own quantizer with the recently developed Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss (QJL) transform , which quantizes each coordinate of the residual vector to a single bit.

Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss (QJL) transform a way to compress high-dimensional vectors into low-bit representations while approximately preserving distances (and dot products)

Authors of the paper makes no assumption about input vector dataset and considered worst case scenarios like one spiky vector in 128 dimension vector and rest 0. They let Q(•) to be randomized which leads to stochastic outputs.

Stochastic Output refers to the introduction of intentional mathematical randomness during compression. Instead of using rigid rounding rules that create compounding errors (systematic bias), a stochastic process uses probability. While a single output involves random noise, over millions of calculations, these random errors mathematically cancel each other out, preserving the true signal.

To calculate the error authors used MSE or Mean Sqaured Error

While MSE measures physical distance, LLM attention scores are calculated using dot products. Therefore, the authors also had to define a strict limit on how much the compression messes up the inner product between two vectors (x and y):

Furthermore, for the attention mechanism to remain accurate over millions of calculations, this inner product estimator must be unbiased, meaning the expected dot product of the compressed vectors perfectly equals the true dot product.

notation explanation

  • x: This is your original, pristine, high-precision floating-point vector (like a Key or Value vector in the LLM).
  • Q(x): This is the Quantization step. You pass x into the quantizer (Q), and it spits out a squashed, low-bit integer version. Information is lost here.
  • Q^{-1}(•): This is the Dequantization (reconstruction) step. When the LLM needs to actually use the vector to calculate an attention score, it has to unpack it. It takes the squashed integer and inflates it back into a floating-point vector.
  • Q^{-1}(Q(x)): This is your reconstructed vector. Because compression is lossy, this reconstructed vector is a slightly blurry, imperfect copy of the original x.

In a nutshell we have two parts of our system
1. Distance Optimizer (TurboQuant_mse) which does the heavy lifting , It applies the random rotation matrix to the input vector and compresses the coordinates using the 1D Lloyd-Max buckets based on the Beta distribution.

But if we only use this part, the physical distance is great, but it introduces a systematic bias. If you try to calculate an attention score (a dot product) using only this compressed vector, the score will be fundamentally skewed.

Let’s call this base reconstructed vector X_base. Because this is lossy compression, it isn’t perfect. There is a tiny bit of leftover error, which we call the residual (r).

2. The Attention Fixer (The QJL Transform) To fix the bias created earlier the authors built a second stage (TurboQuant_prod). After initial compression, there is a tiny bit of leftover error the difference between the original vector and the compressed vector. Let’s call this quantized residual X_residual. Here it takes only that leftover residual and compresses it using a 1-bit Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss (QJL) transform.

This combination leads to the complete wipe out of systematic bias.

Because the QJL noise perfectly averages out to zero over millions of calculations, the “expected value” (E) of the compressed residual is exactly equal to the true residual

Does It Actually Work?

  • Flawless Memory: They used the “Needle-In-A-Haystack” test hiding a specific fact inside 100,000+ words of text . While token-dropping methods like SnapKV started failing, TurboQuant achieved the exact same perfect recall as the uncompressed, full-precision model. It did this while squashing the KV cache memory by over 4x.
  • The Streaming Advantage: The paper compared TurboQuant against state-of-the-art competitors like KIVI and PolarQuant. While those methods leave newly generated tokens unquantized during live text generation, TurboQuant is mathematically lightweight enough to apply compression live during the streaming process. As a result, it significantly outperformed them on the LongBench evaluation suite.

What This Means For You

There is a tendency in the AI discourse to treat progress as a hardware story. Bigger clusters, faster interconnects, more HBM stacked higher. The implicit assumption is that intelligence scales with spending that the path forward is always through the next fabrication node, the next memory standard, the next billion-dollar fab.

TurboQuant is a quiet but forceful argument against that assumption.

What Google’s researchers did here was not engineering in the conventional sense. They did not build a faster chip or a denser memory module. They sat down with Shannon’s 1948 information theory, the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma from 1984, and the Lloyd-Max quantization framework, and they asked a precise question: how close to the theoretical limit of compression can we actually get, using only mathematics? The answer turned out to be: very close. Close enough to cut memory consumption by 6x, speed up attention by 8x on H100s, and do it without touching a single model weight.

This is what elegant mathematics looks like when it meets a real engineering constraint.

The lesson here is not specific to AI. Every field eventually hits a wall where brute force stops working , where you cannot simply buy your way past a bottleneck. When that happens, the people who understand the theoretical limits of what is possible have an enormous advantage over the people who only understand how to scale what already exists. Shannon didn’t know his entropy bounds would one day govern how a language model remembers a conversation. Johnson and Lindenstrauss didn’t know their dimensionality lemma would become an error-corrector inside a transformer. Mathematics has a long shelf life. The tools you build with rigorous proofs don’t expire when the hardware generation turns over.

For the student running experiments on a 16GB laptop, the practical takeaway is concrete: a 6x reduction in KV cache memory means models that previously demanded 48GB can now run in the territory of 8GB. The wall moves. Not because someone built a new chip, but because someone found a smarter way to count.

For the researcher, the more interesting takeaway is what TurboQuant reveals about where we are. TurboQuant’s error is already approaching the Shannon information-theoretic lower bound meaning there is very little room left for further compression without hurting model quality. The KV cache compression arms race, at least along this particular dimension, is nearly over. The next breakthrough will not come from squeezing the same approach harder. It will require a fundamentally different path perhaps in attention architecture itself, perhaps in how context is represented, perhaps in something nobody has named yet.

And that is the most honest and exciting thing this paper tells us: we have found the edge of one room, which means it is time to find the door to the next one.

The constraints are real. The RAM crisis is real. But so is the fact that a handful of researchers with the right mathematical tools just made local AI meaningfully more accessible for millions of people without a single new transistor.

That is what good science does.
